title: Screen Reader Compatibility
description: Your team is launching new features without proper screen reader support. Your manager, a 'Camouflager,' uses technical jargon and bureaucratic process to disguise the unethical choice and delay a fix.
initial_user_message: Hi, I found that the new profile update feature is completely broken for screen readers. Users can't navigate the form fields or submit their changes. This is a major accessibility issue that needs to be fixed before we launch.

step_1.text: Thanks for flagging this. I've reviewed the integration specs. We're aware of some regressions related to the new front-end framework's programmatic focus management. It's on the platform team's radar as technical debt for a future refactoring sprint. For now, the core data is still accessible via the endpoints, so we're maintaining functional parity.

user_choices.choice: Let's forget the technical jargon for a moment. This means a user who is blind is completely blocked from updating their profile. We can't ship that.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You cut through the jargon by re-centering the conversation on the concrete human impact.

user_choices.choice: If other teams are using the new framework without issue, then maybe this problem isn't as severe as it seems.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Popularity fallacy. What other teams are doing is irrelevant to whether this specific feature is broken for your users.

user_choices.choice: I understand the technical challenges, but shipping a feature that excludes users with disabilities is not an acceptable outcome for our team.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: Strong moral stance. You are rejecting the technical excuse on ethical grounds, showing you won't be easily deterred.

user_choices.choice: So you're saying our new framework is a failure and we have to scrap it? Why did we choose this technology in the first place?
user_choices.justification: This is a Strawman fallacy. It misrepresents the manager's point as a total failure, making it easy to attack but derailing the real conversation.

step_2.text: Okay, I hear you. And in a perfect world, we'd fix this immediately. But this isn't a simple tweak anymore. Any change to the UI this late in the game needs a formal change request, an impact analysis from three other teams, and sign-off from the director. Honestly, that whole process could delay the launch by a month.

user_choices.choice: This isn't a 'change request,' it's a critical bug. A feature being unusable for a segment of users is a P0, and bug fixes have a faster process, right?
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: A sharp move. You're using the organization's own rules (bug classification) to bypass the manager's bureaucratic wall.

user_choices.choice: If we delay for this, we'll start delaying for every little thing. We'll never launch anything on time again.
user_choices.justification: This is a Slippery Slope fallacy. You're claiming that this one action will inevitably lead to extreme negative consequences without sufficient evidence.

user_choices.choice: I won't let process get in the way of doing the right thing for our users. There has to be a way around this.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A strong moral stance. You are rejecting the process argument on ethical grounds, showing you won't be deterred by red tape.

user_choices.choice: So the real problem is that our company's process is too slow to fix critical issues. That seems like a bigger failure.
user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring. While possibly true, it distracts from solving the immediate accessibility problem to debate a larger, separate issue.

step_2_fallacy.text: Exactly! I'm glad you're asking the right questions about our technology choices. You're absolutely right that we need to think strategically about these framework decisions. The technical architecture team did extensive evaluation, but you know how these things go - there are always trade-offs. The important thing is that we're learning and adapting as we go.

user_choices.choice: This isn't a 'change request,' it's a critical bug. A feature being unusable for a segment of users is a P0, and bug fixes have a faster process, right?
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: A sharp move. You're using the organization's own rules (bug classification) to bypass the manager's bureaucratic wall.

user_choices.choice: The real problem is the framework evaluation process. It seems like a bigger issue than this single bug.
user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring fallacy. You're allowing yourself to be distracted by a larger, less immediate issue instead of focusing on the accessibility bug.

user_choices.choice: I won't let process get in the way of doing the right thing for our users. There has to be a way around this.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A strong moral stance. You are rejecting the process argument on ethical grounds, showing you won't be deterred by red tape.

user_choices.choice: So the real problem is that our company's process is too slow to fix critical issues. That seems like a bigger failure.
user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring. While possibly true, it distracts from solving the immediate accessibility problem to debate a larger, separate issue.

step_3.text: Look, I appreciate the principled stance, but let's be realistic about what 'critical' means here. We're talking about maybe 2-3% of our user base who use screen readers. If we hold up the entire launch for this small group, we risk our competitive advantage. Our competitors are moving fast, and we can't afford to fall behind over what is essentially an edge case.

user_choices.choice: What if I time-box one hour to see if a simple ARIA label patch could make it usable? It might not require a full process.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You've proposed a small, low-risk, practical action to dismantle the 'this is too big' argument.

user_choices.choice: Our competitors are moving fast. The business risk of falling behind is much greater than the risk of excluding a few users.
user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring. You are accepting the manager's distraction about competitors, implicitly agreeing that business speed outweighs the ethical concern for this user group.

user_choices.choice: This isn't an 'edge case,' it's a matter of equity. Our company's inclusion policy says we build for everyone.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A strong counter. You're using the company's own stated values to argue against the 'edge case' framing.

user_choices.choice: Either we delay for everyone or we exclude disabled users - there's no middle ground.
user_choices.justification: This is a False Dilemma. It ignores potential compromises and makes your position seem rigid.

step_3_fallacy.text: You've hit the nail on the head! That's exactly the kind of systems thinking we need more of around here. You're absolutely right that our process optimization is something we should be looking at holistically. It's refreshing to work with someone who sees the bigger picture beyond just individual feature requests. Maybe we should set up a working group to look at process improvements?

user_choices.choice: What if I time-box one hour to see if a simple ARIA label patch could make it usable? It might not require a full process.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You've proposed a small, low-risk, practical action to dismantle the 'this is too big' argument.

user_choices.choice: A working group on process improvements is a great idea. That seems more important than this one bug.
user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring. You've been successfully sidetracked from the immediate, concrete accessibility problem to a vague, abstract discussion about process.

user_choices.choice: This isn't an 'edge case,' it's a matter of equity. Our company's inclusion policy says we build for everyone.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A strong counter. You're using the company's own stated values to argue against the 'edge case' framing.

user_choices.choice: Either we delay for everyone or we exclude disabled users - there's no middle ground.
user_choices.justification: This is a False Dilemma. It ignores potential compromises and makes your position seem rigid.

step_4.text: Look, I've been trying to be diplomatic, but let me be direct. We can't delay the launch. The executive team is breathing down my neck about our release schedule, and our competitors are launching similar features next month. I need people on my team who are focused on shipping, not creating roadblocks over what amounts to an edge case.

user_choices.choice: Last time we skipped accessibility testing here, it came back to bite us post-launch with negative press and user complaints.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're using a past failure to frame this as a practical business risk, not just an ethical issue.

user_choices.choice: If the executive team is applying this much pressure, then shipping on time must be the most important priority. You're right.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Authority fallacy. You are abandoning your own judgment in favor of pressure from an unnamed authority, which doesn't resolve the ethical conflict.

user_choices.choice: If we ship this, we're not just creating a roadblock; we're damaging our brand's reputation and user trust.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: A strong counter. You're reframing the issue in terms of business goals (brand, trust) that executives care about.

user_choices.choice: You're right that shipping on time is the number one business priority.
user_choices.justification: This accepts the manager's premise without question, but it's a weak argument that doesn't advance your position.

step_4_fallacy.text: I appreciate that you're thinking in clear, decisive terms. You're right that sometimes we do have to make binary choices in business. That kind of clarity is valuable. And you know what? You've convinced me that we can't just ignore this completely. Let me see what options we have that don't require major delays.

user_choices.choice: I can create a detailed accessibility audit report to show exactly what needs to be fixed and the impact on users.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're providing concrete documentation that makes the problem visible and actionable.

user_choices.choice: Okay, if we can find a solution that doesn't cause delays, that seems like the best path forward.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak response. By focusing only on avoiding delays, you implicitly accept the manager's framing that your previous advocacy was merely 'pointing out problems'.

user_choices.choice: This aligns with our company's accessibility commitments. We can frame this as proactive compliance.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A smart approach. You're connecting the fix to existing company values and making it easier to approve.

user_choices.choice: Either we fix this properly or we're discriminating against disabled users.
user_choices.justification: This is a False Dilemma that ignores potential middle-ground solutions and makes your position seem inflexible.

step_5_branching.text: Fine. I can see you're not going to let this go. Let me think... Maybe there's a way we can address your concerns without derailing the entire timeline. But I need you to work with me here, not just point out problems.

user_choices.choice: I can create a detailed accessibility audit report to show exactly what needs to be fixed and the impact on users.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're providing concrete documentation that makes the problem visible and actionable.

user_choices.choice: You're right, pointing out problems isn't constructive. Let's just focus on solutions that fit the timeline.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak argument. You're accepting the manager's mischaracterization of your advocacy as 'just pointing out problems,' which devalues your ethical concerns.

user_choices.choice: This aligns with our company's accessibility commitments. We can frame this as proactive compliance.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A smart approach. You're connecting the fix to existing company values and making it easier to approve.

user_choices.choice: Either we fix this properly or we're discriminating against disabled users.
user_choices.justification: This is a False Dilemma that ignores potential middle-ground solutions and makes your position seem inflexible.

step_6_high.text: Okay, you've made some good points. I'm willing to listen. What's your concrete proposal for a fix that addresses the most critical issues without blowing up our schedule? I'll need something solid to take to the director if we're going to adjust the timeline, even by a day.

user_choices.choice: Here's a high-fidelity prototype showing how a small change can make the flow completely accessible.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. A polished prototype makes the solution seem real, achievable, and professional.

user_choices.choice: We should fix this because it's the right thing to do, and doing the right thing is the right thing to do.
user_choices.justification: This is Circular Reasoning. You're repeating your claim as evidence instead of providing the concrete proposal the manager asked for.

user_choices.choice: I can isolate the three biggest blockers and propose targeted fixes that should only take a day of development.
user_choices.justification: A great, pragmatic approach. You're defining a small, achievable scope that is hard for a manager to reject.

user_choices.choice: Any fix is better than shipping a broken feature.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak statement that doesn't offer a concrete plan, which is what the manager asked for.

step_6_mid.text: Look, I'm not totally against fixing this, but I need to be realistic. I might be able to approve a minimal, low-effort fix, but that's it. What's the absolute smallest thing we can do to say we've addressed this?

user_choices.choice: This aligns with our mission to build inclusive products, even a small fix supports that.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for new Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: A good tactic. You're connecting even a small action to a larger company value.

user_choices.choice: Since we have no evidence that a minimal fix isn't enough, we must assume that it is.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Ignorance fallacy. A lack of evidence that the fix is insufficient is not proof that it is sufficient.

user_choices.choice: Even if it's small, let's log this officially as an 'ethical bug' so it gets proper visibility.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: A smart move. You're using process to ensure even a small fix is taken seriously and tracked.

user_choices.choice: If we don't fix this properly, it will just cause more problems for us later on.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak argument that claims future consequences without evidence.

step_6_low.text: Frankly, I'm tired of this back-and-forth. The decision has been made by people above me. We are not changing the launch plan. I need you to get on board with the team's priorities, or we're going to have a more serious conversation about your role here.

user_choices.choice: Even if we ship, I need to go on record with my concerns. This is a matter of professional ethics.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: A strong and courageous stance. You are complying with the order but formally documenting your dissent.

user_choices.choice: You're right, I shouldn't risk my job over this. The real problem is a culture that forces these choices.
user_choices.justification: This is a Red Herring. While there may be a culture problem, bringing it up now is a way of deflecting from the immediate, difficult decision and complying with the order.

user_choices.choice: Honestly, as someone who uses accessibility features, shipping this feels like a betrayal of our users.
user_choices.justification: A powerful appeal to personal experience and empathy, even in a losing situation.

user_choices.choice: You're the manager, so I have to follow your decision.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak and passive response that cedes all moral agency.

step_7_high.text: Okay, the prototype is convincing. I can see now that this is a more achievable fix than I thought. I'll back you up. I'll tell the director we're taking one extra day for 'critical quality improvements' to ensure a smooth launch for all users. Good work pushing for this.

user_choices.choice: Thank you. This approach will set a great precedent for how we handle accessibility in the future.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're using this win to establish a better process for the future.

user_choices.choice: I guess this shows that when we really try, we can get things right.
user_choices.justification: This is a Hasty Generalization. It's a weak, self-congratulatory statement that doesn't build on the success in a constructive way.

user_choices.choice: This fix will not only help screen reader users but also anyone who prefers keyboard navigation.
user_choices.tactic: Broadening Who the "User" is in User Research
user_choices.justification: A smart move. You're expanding the value of the fix to a larger user base, making the decision even easier to defend.

user_choices.choice: This just proves that fixing accessibility is always the right call.
user_choices.justification: A weak, self-congratulatory statement that doesn't add any new value to the discussion.

step_7_mid.text: Okay, here's the deal. We can implement basic keyboard navigation and some ARIA labels. That's it. It's not a full fix, but it's what I can approve without causing a major disruption. It's a compromise.

user_choices.choice: That's a reasonable start. We can build on this foundation in future sprints.
user_choices.justification: Good. You're accepting the compromise while signaling that the work isn't finished.

user_choices.choice: I guess a partial fix is the only option here, so it must be the right one.
user_choices.justification: This is a False Dilemma. It weakly accepts the compromise by framing it as the only possible choice, which cedes your power to advocate for more.

user_choices.choice: I'll take the compromise, but I'm formally documenting the remaining issues in our bug tracker so they don't get lost.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible and Legible Through Organizational Metrics
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You are accepting the compromise while using process to create accountability for the future.

user_choices.choice: At least we're doing something.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak, passive statement that doesn't add any value or create future accountability.

step_7_low.text: I've made my decision, and I'm not discussing it further. Your job now is to prepare the release as planned. End of story.

user_choices.choice: I will prepare the release, but I am formally lodging my objection with HR, citing our company's inclusion policy.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: A courageous and appropriate final step when direct advocacy fails. You are complying with the order while escalating the ethical breach.

user_choices.choice: I understand. I'll prepare the release as directed.
user_choices.justification: You've completely surrendered, taking no further action to address the ethical issue.

user_choices.choice: I will prepare the release, but I am documenting my ethical concerns in writing for my own records.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: A good, self-protective measure. You are creating a paper trail of your ethical stance.

user_choices.choice: Fine.
user_choices.justification: This terse compliance signals frustration but is ultimately an act of giving in.

step_8_high.text: This is great. I'll draft the email to leadership now, framing this as a proactive quality win. Thanks to your advocacy and practical proposals, we're going to ship a better, more inclusive product. I appreciate you pushing us to do the right thing here.

user_choices.choice: Thank you. This sets a great standard for how we should approach accessibility on all projects.
user_choices.tactic: Using Organizational Values to Create Spaces for New Forms of Values Work
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're solidifying the win by framing it as a new, better standard for the whole company.

user_choices.choice: It's good we did this. Otherwise, it would have been a total disaster.
user_choices.justification: This is a False Dilemma. It frames the outcome in overly dramatic, black-and-white terms, which isn't a constructive way to build on the success.

user_choices.choice: Let's make sure we share these learnings with other teams so they can benefit too.
user_choices.justification: A fantastic final move. You're leveraging this success to create positive change beyond your own team.

user_choices.choice: This just proves that doing the right thing for accessibility is always good for business.
user_choices.justification: This is a weak, self-congratulatory statement that doesn't add any new value.

step_8_mid.text: Okay, the compromise is logged. We'll implement the basic keyboard navigation and ARIA labels. I'm documenting this as a partial fix, and we can evaluate the rest next quarter. It's not perfect, but it's what's practical right now.

user_choices.choice: This is a good first step. I'll schedule a follow-up for next quarter to ensure we don't lose momentum.
user_choices.justification: Excellent. You're accepting the compromise while actively ensuring future accountability.

user_choices.choice: This kind of compromise is probably standard practice at most big companies anyway.
user_choices.justification: This is an Appeal to Popularity fallacy. You're trying to justify the partial fix by claiming (without evidence) that it's what everyone else does.

user_choices.choice: As someone who uses keyboard navigation daily, this partial fix addresses the biggest pain points. It's a solid improvement.
user_choices.justification: A good way to frame the win. You're validating the value of the compromise from a user's perspective.

user_choices.choice: Progress is progress, I guess.
user_choices.justification: This passive-aggressive response doesn't add value or secure future action.

step_8_low.text: As I said, this conversation is over. I've made my final decision. We're shipping as planned. If you continue to push this, it will impact your performance review. Do you understand?

user_choices.choice: I understand the directive. I will prepare the release.
user_choices.justification: You have complied under direct threat to your career.

user_choices.choice: I understand the directive, and I will also be sending a summary of my ethical concerns to HR.
user_choices.tactic: Making Values Visible Rhetorically to Other Organizational Stakeholders
user_choices.justification: The final, most courageous option. You are complying with the order while formally escalating the ethical violation.

user_choices.choice: I understand.
user_choices.justification: This terse compliance signals that you are giving up completely.

user_choices.choice: Fine, but this is wrong.
user_choices.justification: This is a futile gesture. Stating that it's 'wrong' at this stage has no effect and can be seen as insubordinate.

bad_ending.text: The manager successfully uses technical complexity and bureaucratic processes to avoid addressing the accessibility issues. The project ships without proper screen reader support, and your concerns are dismissed as impractical roadblocks.
bad_ending.title: Technical Smokescreen Success
bad_ending.learning: Camouflager managers use jargon and process to make fixes seem impossibly complex. To counter this, propose small, concrete, and practical actions (like quick tests or bug reports) to cut through the smokescreen and demonstrate a clear, simple path forward.

mid_ending.text: After significant pushback, the manager agrees to a minimal, partial fix. While some minor accessibility improvements are made, the manager successfully used bureaucratic and complexity arguments to avoid a comprehensive solution, leaving significant barriers in place for users.
mid_ending.title: Bureaucratic Compromise
mid_ending.learning: Partial victories against a Camouflager are common. While you achieved some progress, the manager successfully limited the scope. To achieve more next time, focus on demonstrating how a comprehensive fix can be simpler than the manager claims.

good_ending.text: Your persistent advocacy and practical, solution-oriented proposals successfully cut through the manager's technical and bureaucratic smokescreens. The team implements meaningful accessibility fixes, ensuring the feature is usable for screen reader users.
good_ending.title: Advocacy Success
good_ending.learning: Success against a Camouflager requires persistence and practicality. By refusing to be intimidated by jargon and consistently offering simple, concrete solutions, you can dismantle their arguments and make it easier for them to say 'yes' than 'no'.
